Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] MFA push fatigue followed by approved sign-in from new IP (Muddled Libra pattern)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Global Admin role assigned within 60 min of user's first interactive sign-in · [LLM] VM/disk provisioned by identity elevated to admin in last 24h (rogue cloud asset) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
MFA push fatigue followed by approved sign-in from new IP (Muddled Libra pattern) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the Scattered Spider / Muddled Libra initial-access pattern called out in the article: a burst of failed MFA challenges against one user followed within minutes by a successful MFA-required sign-in from an IP that did NOT appear in the failures — i.e., the prompt was approved from a different device/geo than the attacker was hammering from. Rationale: Article explicitly cites 'MFA manipulation' and Muddled Libra/Scattered Spider; kill-chain phase-1 hint calls for 'burst of failed MFA prompts followed by an approval from a new device/geo'. ResultType codes 50074/50076/500121/50158 are the canonical Entra MFA-challenge failures. Joining failures to a successful MFA sign-in from an IP NOT in the failure set is what differentiates push-fatigue from a forgetful user.
ATT&CKT1621 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user mistyped MFA code 5+ times then completed via mobile app from cellular IP (different IP than corp WiFi)
  • User changing networks (office → home VPN → home WiFi) mid-MFA flow
  • Number-matching rollouts where users initially fail then succeed once they understand the new prompt
  • Conditional access policy testing by IAM admins
  • Mobile MFA app retried from different cellular tower IPs in metro areas
Suppression filter
and SuccessIP !startswith "10." and SuccessIP !startswith "192.168." and DeviceDetail.trustType !in ("AzureAdJoined","Hybrid Azure AD joined","AzureAdRegistered")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AccountUpn's last 24h of sign-ins — are the failed IPs from a known hostile ASN/country while the success IP is corporate? Check DeviceDetail.trustType (Compliant/AzureAdJoined) on the success — unmanaged device is a strong escalation signal. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens for the user (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), reset password, require MFA re-registration, and quarantine the success-IP device if it's enrolled. 3) Hunt: from the success-IP, pivot through SigninLogs and AuditLogs for any inbox-rule creation, app-consent grants, role assignments or service-principal credentials added in the next 60 minutes — these are the standard Muddled Libra post-compromise actions.
let WindowMin = 10m;
let Threshold = 5;
let Failures = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode in (50074, 50076, 500121, 50158)
    | summarize FailedCount = count(), FailedIPs = make_set(IPAddress) by AccountUpn, FailWindow = bin(Timestamp, WindowMin);
let Successes = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | where AuthenticationRequirement =~ "multiFactorAuthentication"
    | project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, SuccessIP = IPAddress, Country, City, DeviceName, Application;
Failures
| where FailedCount >= Threshold
| join kind=inner Successes on AccountUpn
| where SuccessTime between (FailWindow .. FailWindow + WindowMin)
| where SuccessIP !in (FailedIPs)
| project SuccessTime, AccountUpn, FailedCount, FailedIPs, SuccessIP, Country, City, DeviceName, Application
| order by SuccessTime desc
let WindowMin = 10m;
let Threshold = 5;
let Failures = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType in (50074, 50076, 500121, 50158)
    | summarize FailedCount = count(), FailedIPs = make_set(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName, FailWindow = bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMin);
let Successes = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | where AuthenticationRequirement =~ "multiFactorAuthentication"
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SuccessIP = IPAddress, LocationDetails, DeviceDetail, AppDisplayName;
Failures
| where FailedCount >= Threshold
| join kind=inner Successes on UserPrincipalName
| where SuccessTime between (FailWindow .. FailWindow + WindowMin)
| where SuccessIP !in (FailedIPs)
| project SuccessTime, UserPrincipalName, FailedCount, FailedIPs, SuccessIP, LocationDetails, DeviceDetail, AppDisplayName
| order by SuccessTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:(50074 OR 50076 OR 500121 OR 50158)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count as mfa_failures values(Authentication.src) as failed_ips from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="failure" (Authentication.signature_id="50074" OR Authentication.signature_id="50076" OR Authentication.signature_id="500121" OR Authentication.signature_id="50158") earliest=-7d by Authentication.user _time span=10m | where mfa_failures >= 5 | rename Authentication.user as user, _time as fail_window | join type=inner user [| tstats summariesonly=true earliest(_time) as success_time values(Authentication.src) as success_ip from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" earliest=-7d by Authentication.user | rename Authentication.user as user] | where success_time >= fail_window AND success_time <= relative_time(fail_window, "+10m") | eval new_ip=if(isnull(mvfind(failed_ips, success_ip)),"yes","no") | where new_ip="yes" | table fail_window success_time user mfa_failures failed_ips success_ip
| tstats summariesonly=false count as mfa_failures values(Authentication.src) as failed_ips from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="failure" (Authentication.signature_id="50074" OR Authentication.signature_id="50076" OR Authentication.signature_id="500121" OR Authentication.signature_id="50158") earliest=-7d by Authentication.user _time span=10m | where mfa_failures >= 5 | rename Authentication.user as user, _time as fail_window | join type=inner user [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as success_time values(Authentication.src) as success_ip from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" earliest=-7d by Authentication.user | rename Authentication.user as user] | where success_time >= fail_window AND success_time <= relative_time(fail_window, "+10m") | eval new_ip=if(isnull(mvfind(failed_ips, success_ip)),"yes","no") | where new_ip="yes" | table fail_window success_time user mfa_failures failed_ips success_ip
Global Admin role assigned within 60 min of user's first interactive sign-in AIInstallation High
Detects the privilege-escalation pattern the article specifically calls out: 'attackers frequently attempt privilege escalation and administrative account abuse within minutes or hours of gaining access.' Hunts users who receive a Privileged/Global Admin role assignment within 60 minutes of their first observed successful sign-in in the lookback window — a shape almost no legitimate onboarding produces. Rationale: Article: 'attackers frequently attempt privilege escalation and administrative account abuse within minutes or hours of gaining access.' Kill-chain phase-2 hint specifically calls for 'New role assignments to Global/Privileged Admin... within minutes of first logon.' First-sign-in→privileged-role-assignment within 60min is a shape legitimate IT onboarding rarely produces (admins usually pre-exist, role assignments happen during business hours after onboarding tickets). Privileged role list drawn from Entra's documented high-impact roles.
ATT&CKT1098 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin onboarding script that creates a user and immediately assigns Global Admin during break-glass account provisioning
  • PIM activation (eligible→active role) which can appear similar in AuditLogs depending on tenant config
  • Tenant migration tooling that imports users and applies role mappings in bulk
  • Service-principal automated provisioning by Workday/SailPoint after first sign-in callback
  • MSP/CSP delegated admin tenant onboarding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatorUpn !in~ (dynamic(["breakglass1@contoso.onmicrosoft.com","breakglass2@contoso.onmicrosoft.com"])) | where TargetUpn !has "#EXT#" | where not (InitiatorUpn endswith "sailpoint.com" or InitiatorUpn has "workday")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatorUpn — is it a known IAM admin or another newly-elevated account (chain elevation)? Pull the TargetUpn's full SigninLogs since FirstSignIn — is the geo/ASN/device consistent with a real employee or with the FirstIP only? Check PIM logs for whether this was an eligible→active activation or a hard role grant. 2) Contain: remove the role assignment, revoke refresh tokens for TargetUpn (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password + MFA re-registration, and block sign-in pending review. If InitiatorUpn looks compromised, contain that account too. 3) Hunt: from TargetUpn within the next 24h pivot AzureActivity for VM/disk creation, service-principal creation, conditional access policy changes, and app consent grants — those are the standard post-elevation actions for Muddled Libra and Spoiled Scorpius per the article.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMin = 60m;
let PrivRoles = dynamic(["Global Administrator","Privileged Role Administrator","Security Administrator","Application Administrator","Cloud Application Administrator","Privileged Authentication Administrator"]);
let RoleAdds = CloudAppEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where Application =~ "Office 365" or Application has "Azure"
    | where ActionType in ("Add member to role.","Add eligible member to role.")
    | extend RoleName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ModifiedProperties[1].NewValue)
    | extend TargetUpn = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).ObjectId)
    | where RoleName has_any (PrivRoles) or tostring(ActivityObjects) has_any (PrivRoles)
    | project AssignTime = Timestamp, TargetUpn, RoleName, InitiatorUpn = AccountDisplayName;
let FirstSignIn = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ErrorCode == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | summarize FirstSignIn = min(Timestamp), FirstIP = arg_min(Timestamp, IPAddress, Country) by AccountUpn;
RoleAdds
| join kind=inner FirstSignIn on $left.TargetUpn == $right.AccountUpn
| where AssignTime between (FirstSignIn .. FirstSignIn + WindowMin)
| extend MinutesElapsed = datetime_diff('minute', AssignTime, FirstSignIn)
| project AssignTime, FirstSignIn, MinutesElapsed, TargetUpn, RoleName, InitiatorUpn, FirstIP, Country
| order by AssignTime desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMin = 60m;
let PrivRoles = dynamic(["Global Administrator","Privileged Role Administrator","Security Administrator","Application Administrator","Cloud Application Administrator","Privileged Authentication Administrator"]);
let RoleAdds = AuditLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OperationName has_any ("Add member to role", "Add eligible member to role")
    | mv-expand TargetResources
    | extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources.userPrincipalName)
    | extend ModifiedProps = TargetResources.modifiedProperties
    | mv-expand ModifiedProps
    | extend PropName = tostring(ModifiedProps.displayName), NewValue = tostring(ModifiedProps.newValue)
    | where PropName has_any ("Role.DisplayName","Role.TemplateId") or NewValue has_any (PrivRoles)
    | extend RoleName = tostring(parse_json(NewValue))
    | where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
    | project AssignTime = TimeGenerated, TargetUpn, RoleName, InitiatorUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), InitiatorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
let FirstSignIn = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ResultType == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | summarize FirstSignIn = min(TimeGenerated), FirstIP = any(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName;
RoleAdds
| join kind=inner FirstSignIn on $left.TargetUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where AssignTime between (FirstSignIn .. FirstSignIn + WindowMin)
| extend MinutesElapsed = datetime_diff('minute', AssignTime, FirstSignIn)
| project AssignTime, FirstSignIn, MinutesElapsed, TargetUpn, RoleName, InitiatorUpn, InitiatorIP, FirstIP
| order by AssignTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("Add member to role" OR "Add eligible member to role") @properties.targetResources.modifiedProperties.newValue:(*"Global Administrator"* OR *"Privileged Role Administrator"* OR *"Application Administrator"* OR *"Cloud Application Administrator"* OR *"Privileged Authentication Administrator"*)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true earliest(_time) as first_signin from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.app="Azure Active Directory" earliest=-7d by Authentication.user | rename Authentication.user as user | join type=inner user [| tstats summariesonly=true earliest(_time) as role_assign_time values(All_Changes.object) as role from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action="modified" All_Changes.change_type="AAA" (All_Changes.object="Global Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Privileged Role Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Security Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Application Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Cloud Application Administrator") earliest=-7d by All_Changes.user | rename All_Changes.user as user] | eval minutes_elapsed=round((role_assign_time-first_signin)/60,1) | where minutes_elapsed >= 0 AND minutes_elapsed <= 60 | table first_signin role_assign_time minutes_elapsed user role
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as first_signin from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.app="Azure Active Directory" earliest=-7d by Authentication.user | rename Authentication.user as user | join type=inner user [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as role_assign_time values(All_Changes.object) as role from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action="modified" All_Changes.change_type="AAA" (All_Changes.object="Global Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Privileged Role Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Security Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Application Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Cloud Application Administrator") earliest=-7d by All_Changes.user | rename All_Changes.user as user] | eval minutes_elapsed=round((role_assign_time-first_signin)/60,1) | where minutes_elapsed >= 0 AND minutes_elapsed <= 60 | table first_signin role_assign_time minutes_elapsed user role
VM/disk provisioned by identity elevated to admin in last 24h (rogue cloud asset) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the persistence pattern the article specifically names — 'create rogue virtual machines, mount virtual drives' — by joining Entra role-assignment audit events to AzureActivity VM/disk write operations within 24h of elevation. The article calls this out as a distinct Muddled Libra / Spoiled Scorpius behaviour for staging exfiltration. Rationale: Article body: 'they may provision cloud resources, create rogue virtual machines, mount virtual drives or establish persistence to support data staging and exfiltration.' Kill-chain phase-5 hint: 'Creation of new VMs/disks in unexpected regions.' The join — Entra role grant → AzureActivity compute write within 24h by the same identity — is the article-specific shape. beginGetAccess/snapshots/extensions cover the disk-mounting and runtime-extension abuse that's harder to spot than the VM write itself.
ATT&CKT1578.002 T1098
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine new platform engineer onboarded with Contributor on a sandbox subscription, then immediately spinning up their first VM for testing
  • Cloud migration project where a freshly-elevated admin provisions a fleet of test VMs
  • Infrastructure-as-code service principal granted Contributor and then running Terraform apply
  • PIM eligible→active activation where the user genuinely had standing eligibility and is doing routine work
  • Disaster recovery drills where elevated breakglass accounts spin up replacement VMs
Suppression filter
| where ResourceGroup !has "sandbox" and ResourceGroup !has "-dev-" and ResourceGroup !has "terraform" | where CallerIpAddress !startswith "10." and CallerIpAddress !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the VM/disk's region, size, and image — unfamiliar region or oversized VM (e.g. Standard_E64s_v5 when this tenant runs Standard_D2) is a strong signal. Check the VM's NIC for public IP, NSG rules opening RDP/SSH from internet, and any disk attachments to other VMs (mounted virtual drive pattern). 2) Contain: stop and isolate the VM (deny inbound NSG rule), snapshot disks for forensics BEFORE deletion, revoke the Caller's tokens, and freeze the resource group. 3) Hunt: from the VM look for outbound transfer volume (NSG flow logs, Azure Storage access logs from this VM's identity), any newly-mounted disks belonging to other resource groups, and any storage account key listings (Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action) by Caller — that's the data-staging precursor the article describes.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let PostElevationWindow = 24h;
let PrivRoles = dynamic(["Global Administrator","Privileged Role Administrator","Application Administrator","Cloud Application Administrator"]);
let Elevated = AuditLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OperationName has_any ("Add member to role", "Add eligible member to role")
    | mv-expand TargetResources
    | extend ElevatedUpn = tolower(tostring(TargetResources.userPrincipalName))
    | mv-expand ModifiedProps = TargetResources.modifiedProperties
    | extend NewValue = tostring(ModifiedProps.newValue)
    | where NewValue has_any (PrivRoles)
    | summarize ElevationTime = min(TimeGenerated) by ElevatedUpn;
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where OperationNameValue in~ (
    "MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/VIRTUALMACHINES/WRITE",
    "MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/DISKS/WRITE",
    "MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/DISKS/BEGINGETACCESS/ACTION",
    "MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/SNAPSHOTS/WRITE",
    "MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/VIRTUALMACHINES/EXTENSIONS/WRITE")
| where ActivityStatusValue in ("Started","Succeeded","Success")
| extend CallerLower = tolower(Caller)
| join kind=inner Elevated on $left.CallerLower == $right.ElevatedUpn
| where TimeGenerated between (ElevationTime .. ElevationTime + PostElevationWindow)
| extend MinutesAfterElevation = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, ElevationTime)
| project TimeGenerated, ElevationTime, MinutesAfterElevation, Caller, OperationNameValue, ResourceGroup, _ResourceId, CallerIpAddress, ActivityStatusValue
| order by TimeGenerated asc
source:azure.activity_logs @operationName.value:("Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write" OR "Microsoft.Compute/disks/write" OR "Microsoft.Compute/disks/beginGetAccess/action" OR "Microsoft.Compute/snapshots/write" OR "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write") @properties.activityStatusValue:(Started OR Succeeded OR Success)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true earliest(_time) as elevation_time from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.change_type="AAA" All_Changes.action="modified" (All_Changes.object="Global Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Privileged Role Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Application Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Contributor" OR All_Changes.object="Owner") earliest=-7d by All_Changes.dest_user | rename All_Changes.dest_user as elevated_user | join type=inner elevated_user [| tstats summariesonly=true earliest(_time) as vm_create_time values(All_Changes.object) as cloud_object values(All_Changes.src) as caller_ip from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.change_type="Azure" (All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write" OR All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/disks/write" OR All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/disks/beginGetAccess/action" OR All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/snapshots/write") earliest=-7d by All_Changes.user | rename All_Changes.user as elevated_user] | eval hours_after_elevation=round((vm_create_time-elevation_time)/3600,1) | where hours_after_elevation >= 0 AND hours_after_elevation <= 24 | table elevation_time vm_create_time hours_after_elevation elevated_user cloud_object caller_ip
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as elevation_time from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.change_type="AAA" All_Changes.action="modified" (All_Changes.object="Global Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Privileged Role Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Application Administrator" OR All_Changes.object="Contributor" OR All_Changes.object="Owner") earliest=-7d by All_Changes.dest_user | rename All_Changes.dest_user as elevated_user | join type=inner elevated_user [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) as vm_create_time values(All_Changes.object) as cloud_object values(All_Changes.src) as caller_ip from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.change_type="Azure" (All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write" OR All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/disks/write" OR All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/disks/beginGetAccess/action" OR All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Compute/snapshots/write") earliest=-7d by All_Changes.user | rename All_Changes.user as elevated_user] | eval hours_after_elevation=round((vm_create_time-elevation_time)/3600,1) | where hours_after_elevation >= 0 AND hours_after_elevation <= 24 | table elevation_time vm_create_time hours_after_elevation elevated_user cloud_object caller_ip
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

SecurityEvent

BleepingComputer
2026-06-15 8 use cases 1 technique 6 kill-chain phases detected

A vulnerability in the SimpleHelp remote management software allows unauthenticated attackers to create privileged technician accounts on servers using the OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication protocol. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internet-exposed SimpleHelp servers vulnerable to CVE-2026-48558 · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue SimpleHelp Technician account created via OIDC bypass (CVE-2026-48558) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — SimpleHelp bug lets hackers create rogue remote support accounts
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SimpleHelp 'Remote Access.exe' spawning script interpreters on managed endpoints · [LLM] Newly created SimpleHelp Technician immediately exercises privileged actions
Rogue SimpleHelp Technician account created via OIDC bypass (CVE-2026-48558) AIInstallation High
Detects new Technician account registrations/logons in the SimpleHelp server audit log forwarded as syslog. Targets the exact persistence vector from CVE-2026-48558 where forged OIDC identity assertions register an attacker-controlled privileged Technician without MFA. Rationale: Article explicitly names /opt/SimpleHelp/logs/server.log as the audit trail that records 'technician registrations, email addresses, and configuration changes performed by rogue accounts'. Cross-checked with Horizon3.ai disclosure which calls out IoC review focused on 'new authenticated technician users with unknown or suspicious names and/or email addresses' and confirms OIDC is the bypassed code path. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/ • https://www.securityweek.com/vulnerabilities-in-simplehelp-remote-access-software-may-lead-to-system-compromise/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.004 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new MSP technician onboarded via OIDC SSO and provisioned just-in-time
  • IT bulk-imports staff into a new SimpleHelp Technician Group on first OIDC rollout
  • Test/QA Technician accounts spun up for SimpleHelp version 5.5.16 upgrade verification
  • Existing technician's UPN changes after a HR rename (creates 'new' OIDC identity)
Suppression filter
| where not (NewUser in ("", "system") or Email endswith "@yourcorp.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full server.log block for the new Technician: capture username, email domain, OIDC subject claim, source IP, Technician Group joined, and whether 'Allow group authenticated logins' is enabled on that group; cross-check the username/email against HR/IdP directory. 2) Contain — if the user is not in the IdP directory or the source IP is foreign, immediately disable the Technician account in SimpleHelp, revoke any active sessions, IP-allowlist Technician logins, and verify the server is on 5.5.16 / 6.0RC2 (patch CVE-2026-48558). 3) Hunt — pivot on the same source IP/UA across server.log for prior OIDC probes; review session history for managed-endpoint remote-control or script-execution actions launched by the rogue Technician within the next 24h (feeds UC4).
let LookbackDays = 7d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ProcessName has "SimpleHelp" or SyslogMessage has "SimpleHelp"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Technician", "technician")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("created", "registered", "added", "OIDC login", "new technician")
| extend NewUser = extract(@"(?i)technician[^\w]+([\w._-]+@?[\w._-]*)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Email = extract(@"([\w._%+-]+@[\w.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend OidcFlag = iff(SyslogMessage has "OIDC" or SyslogMessage has "openid", "oidc", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, OidcFlag, NewUser, Email, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:simplehelp (@message:*Technician* OR @message:*technician*) (@message:*created* OR @message:*registered* OR @message:*added* OR @message:*"OIDC login"*) (@message:*OIDC* OR @message:*openid*)
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.user) as user values(Authentication.signature) as signature from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="SimpleHelp" (Authentication.signature IN ("TechnicianCreated","TechnicianRegistered","OIDCLogin","technician_added") OR Authentication.action="success") Authentication.authentication_method="OIDC" by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where firstSeen >= relative_time(now(),"-7d") | eval suspicious=if(match(user, "(?i)(test|admin[0-9]+|temp|qa|root|svc)") OR len(user)<4 OR match(user,"^[a-z0-9]{8,}$"),1,0)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.user) as user values(Authentication.signature) as signature from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="SimpleHelp" (Authentication.signature IN ("TechnicianCreated","TechnicianRegistered","OIDCLogin","technician_added") OR Authentication.action="success") Authentication.authentication_method="OIDC" by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where firstSeen >= relative_time(now(),"-7d") | eval suspicious=if(match(user, "(?i)(test|admin[0-9]+|temp|qa|root|svc)") OR len(user)<4 OR match(user,"^[a-z0-9]{8,}$"),1,0)
SimpleHelp 'Remote Access.exe' spawning script interpreters on managed endpoints AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation pivot from CVE-2026-48558: a rogue Technician using SimpleHelp's 'execute scripts' capability against managed endpoints. Looks for the SimpleHelp customer-client binary spawning shells or LOLBin script interpreters, which is the only on-endpoint signal an attacker leaves when abusing the platform. Rationale: Article describes the SimpleHelp Technician role as 'remoting into managed endpoints, executing scripts, and more' — the only on-endpoint footprint of that abuse is the customer-client binary spawning shells. Binary name 'Remote Access.exe' (vendor 'SimpleHelp LTD') corroborated by Arctic Wolf's prior SimpleHelp campaign write-up — kept generic on installation path because SimpleHelp installs vary per deployment. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/arctic-wolf-observes-campaign-exploiting-simplehelp-rmm-software-for-initial-access/ • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/
ATT&CKT1219 T1059 T1072
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Help-desk technician runs a legitimate cmd/PowerShell command during a support call
  • MSP-pushed scheduled scripts (patch installers, log collectors) launched via SimpleHelp remote session
  • SimpleHelp's built-in 'Tools' menu running diagnostic commands (ipconfig, systeminfo)
  • Endpoint inventory script invoked by IT during fleet audit
  • Vendor-supplied update wrapped as a script and pushed through SimpleHelp
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("\\Get-ComputerInfo", "\\ipconfig", "systeminfo", "\\WindowsUpdate")) and not (AccountName in~ ("known-helpdesk-svc"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full child command line, SHA256, and the Technician name driving the SimpleHelp session from server.log within ±2 min of the spawn; check if the Technician is a known-good IdP user. 2) Contain — if the Technician is unknown / brand-new / has a suspicious email domain, kill the SimpleHelp session, isolate the affected endpoint via MDE, disable the Technician account on the SimpleHelp server, and rotate any creds typed during the session. 3) Hunt — pivot on the Technician's identity across server.log for every other endpoint they touched in the last 14d; sweep those endpoints for the same parent→child pattern, plus newly written persistence artifacts (services, Run keys, scheduled tasks) attributed to 'Remote Access.exe'.
let Lookback = 7d;
let Lolbins = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Remote Access.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("SimpleHelp", "SimpleHelp LTD") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "SimpleHelp"
| where FileName in~ (Lolbins)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 7d;
let Lolbins = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\Remote Access.exe" or ActingProcessName =~ "Remote Access.exe"
| where (ActingProcessFileCompany has_any ("SimpleHelp", "SimpleHelp LTD")) or ActingProcessName has "SimpleHelp"
| extend ChildExe = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where tolower(ChildExe) in (Lolbins)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects the SimpleHelp customer-client process ('Remote Access.exe', SimpleHelp LTD) spawning shells or LOLBin script interpreters. After CVE-2026-48558, rogue OIDC-registered Technicians can drive arbitrary script execution on managed endpoints via this exact chain.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/simplehelp-bug-lets-hackers-create-rogue-remote-support-accounts/
  - https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:

  - attack.t1059

  - attack.execution
  - attack.lateral_movement
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\Remote Access.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'

| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, UserName], function=count())
| count > 0

Internet-exposed SimpleHelp servers vulnerable to CVE-2026-48558 AIReconnaissance High
Asset-surface hunt for SimpleHelp servers running 5.5.15 or older / 6.0 pre-release that are reachable from the internet — the entire prerequisite for CVE-2026-48558 exploitation. Lets the SOC drive emergency patching to 5.5.16 / 6.0RC2 before opportunistic exploitation. Rationale: Article gives the exact patched versions (5.5.16, 6.0RC2 released June 9 2026) and prerequisite (internet-exposed server with OIDC). Detection joins Defender TVM CveId lookup against DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing so SOC can prioritise the ~14,000-server exposure cited by Horizon3.ai's Shodan analysis. Image [3] in the article also visually confirms a rogue Technician landed on a real server console. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-48558
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SimpleHelp servers behind reverse-proxy/WAF that Defender marks as IsInternetFacing but are not directly reachable on 443
  • Lab/test SimpleHelp 6.0 pre-release instances that intentionally lag patches
  • DR-replica SimpleHelp servers visible to TVM but powered off / firewall-blocked
  • Servers patched in the last 24h that TVM hasn't yet re-scanned
Suppression filter
| where IsInternetFacing == true
Response runbook
1) Triage — for each hit, confirm the SimpleHelp version via the server's About page or `/configuration/version`, validate OIDC is enabled, and identify which Technician Groups have 'Allow group authenticated logins' set. 2) Contain — if internet-facing and unpatched, immediately apply 5.5.16 (5.x branch) or 6.0RC2, and as a stop-gap put an IP allowlist on Technician logins per SimpleHelp's mitigation guidance; rotate any technician API tokens. 3) Hunt — pull /opt/SimpleHelp/logs/server.log on each exposed host for any Technician created since 2026-06-01 with an unknown email domain, and run UC1 retroactively for the last 30 days.
let Vulnerable = DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where CveId == "CVE-2026-48558"
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId;
let Exposed = DeviceInfo

| join kind=leftouter Exposed on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,

Vulnerable

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(Vulnerabilities.severity) as severity values(Vulnerabilities.signature) as signature values(Vulnerabilities.vendor_product) as product from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where (Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-48558" OR (Vulnerabilities.vendor_product="SimpleHelp" AND Vulnerabilities.signature="SimpleHelp" AND Vulnerabilities.severity="critical")) by Vulnerabilities.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(Vulnerabilities.severity) as severity values(Vulnerabilities.signature) as signature values(Vulnerabilities.vendor_product) as product from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where (Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-48558" OR (Vulnerabilities.vendor_product="SimpleHelp" AND Vulnerabilities.signature="SimpleHelp" AND Vulnerabilities.severity="critical")) by Vulnerabilities.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
Newly created SimpleHelp Technician immediately exercises privileged actions AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a brand-new Technician registration in SimpleHelp server.log with privileged actions (remote-session start, script execution, group/role change) by that same account within minutes. The compressed timeline is the signature of CVE-2026-48558 abuse — legitimate onboarding flows have a HR/training gap. Rationale: Article emphasises that the rogue Technician is *immediately* usable for 'remoting into managed endpoints, executing scripts'. Kill-chain block phase 4 detection hint: 'Newly created Technician accounts immediately exercising privileged actions ... shortly after first login'. The 15-minute window keeps onboarding-with-immediate-use FPs but eliminates legitimate flows where HR creates the account hours before first use. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1098 T1219
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP runbook that provisions a Technician and immediately runs a smoke-test remote session
  • Migration scripts during the 5.5.16 / 6.0RC2 upgrade that re-create Technicians and validate access
  • Just-in-time access tooling that creates an ephemeral Technician for a single ticket
  • QA engineer creating a Technician and self-testing within minutes
Suppression filter
| where DelaySec >= 5
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture the new Technician's username, email, OIDC sub claim, source IP, and the exact privileged action taken (which managed endpoint did they hit, which script ran). 2) Contain — disable the Technician account in SimpleHelp, kill any in-flight remote sessions to the targeted endpoints, isolate those endpoints via MDE, and snapshot for forensics; if the server is still on a vulnerable version, patch to 5.5.16 / 6.0RC2 immediately. 3) Hunt — for the source IP and OIDC sub claim, enumerate all SimpleHelp authentications and every endpoint the rogue Technician interacted with; on each endpoint, run UC2 retro-active and inspect created services, scheduled tasks, and outbound C2 connections from 'Remote Access.exe' or its children.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMinutes = 15m;
let Creations = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ProcessName has "SimpleHelp" or SyslogMessage has "SimpleHelp"
    | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)technician.*?(created|registered|added)"
    | extend NewUser = extract(@"(?i)technician[^\w]+([\w._-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(NewUser)
    | project CreateTime = TimeGenerated, NewUser, Computer, CreationMsg = SyslogMessage;
let PrivActions = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ProcessName has "SimpleHelp" or SyslogMessage has "SimpleHelp"
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("remote session", "script", "group modified", "configuration changed", "role", "privilege")
    | extend ActorUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:user|technician|by)[^\w]+([\w._-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ActorUser)
    | project ActionTime = TimeGenerated, ActorUser, Computer, ActionMsg = SyslogMessage;
Creations
| join kind=inner (PrivActions) on $left.NewUser == $right.ActorUser
| where ActionTime between (CreateTime .. CreateTime + WindowMinutes)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', ActionTime, CreateTime)
| project CreateTime, ActionTime, DelaySec, NewUser, Computer, CreationMsg, ActionMsg
| order by ActionTime desc

Vitest Browser Mode API launched bound to non-loopback (--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for the precondition of CVE-2026-53633: a Node/Vitest process started with the Browser Mode API server bound to all interfaces, which exposes the WebSocket CDP RPC to the network. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact Vitest CLI/config flag named in the advisory. Rationale: Pivots on the exact configuration in the advisory's reproduction (`api.host: '0.0.0.0'`) combined with the Vitest binary string. No second source — advisory itself, npm:@vitest/browser package metadata. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53633
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineers intentionally testing Vitest browser mode across a LAN dev pairing setup
  • CI/CD agents running Vitest browser tests inside containers where 0.0.0.0 is the standard bind
  • Developer documentation/POC exploration of Vitest after reading the advisory
  • Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners using exposed Vitest for cross-host tests
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ci-runner","build-agent") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("runner.exe","actions-runner.exe"))
Response runbook
Triage: confirm whether host is a developer/CI workstation and whether the Vitest process is still listening — netstat -ano on the parent PID; check if @vitest/browser version is in the vulnerable range (>=3.0.0,<=3.2.4 / >=4.0.0,<=4.1.7 / 5.0.0-beta.0..3). Contain: terminate the node process, ensure firewall blocks inbound 63315 on dev subnet, force upgrade @vitest/browser. Hunt: pivot on DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound traffic to the listener LocalPort and on DeviceFileEvents for any recent modification of vite.config.ts/vitest.config.ts on that host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","pnpm.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","npx.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","@vitest/browser","vite-plus")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)browser\.api\.host[= ]+0\.0\.0\.0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where CommandLine has_any ("vitest","@vitest/browser","vite-plus")
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)browser\.api\.host[= ]+0\.0\.0\.0"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound network connection to Vitest Browser Mode listener (TCP 63315) AIDelivery High
Hunts for remote clients connecting to the Vitest Browser Mode API listener on the documented default port 63315, which only matters when --browser.api.host=0.0.0.0 has been set. Article-specific because 63315 is the literal port the advisory's reproduction binds. Rationale: Port 63315 is the Vitest Browser Mode default named explicitly in the advisory (`http://localhost:63315`). Pairing it with a node-owned listener and non-loopback source IP gives a tight signal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer pairing across LAN intentionally connecting browser to teammate's Vitest
  • CI test orchestrator probing dev pods on 63315
  • Service mesh or proxy mistakenly forwarding 63315 internally
  • Pentester / internal scanning hitting dev workstations
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in (dynamic(["<known-dev-peer-ip>"])) and DeviceName startswith "DEV-")
Response runbook
Triage: identify the RemoteIP — internal known dev peer or unknown? Pull Vitest process lineage on the listener host. Contain: block inbound 63315 at host firewall and on the dev subnet egress filter; restart Vitest with default localhost binding. Hunt: in the next 5 minutes around the inbound, look for vite.config.ts/vitest.config.ts FileModified events on the target host (next UC's logic).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" or ActionType == "ConnectionInbound" or ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort == 63315
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","npx.exe")
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 63315
| where DeviceAction in ("allow","accept","Permit")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP)) or SourceIP != DestinationIP
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, RequestURL, DestinationHostName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vite.config.ts / vitest.config.* overwrite by browser process (CDP download path) AIInstallation High
Detects the exploitation primitive: the project's vite.config.ts/vitest.config.* getting written by a Chromium-family browser process, which is the CDP Page.setDownloadBehavior + Runtime.evaluate chain landing the malicious config in the project root. This is the unique footprint of CVE-2026-53633 exploitation. Rationale: vite.config.ts is the named-overwrite target in the advisory. Browser-process file writes outside Default download/Cache directories — let alone to a TS config in a project root — are pathological and uniquely match the CDP download-redirect primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually saving config via a Vue DevTools / browser-based file-system editor (rare on disk-backed config)
  • Browser auto-restore of a download interrupted earlier (unlikely for .ts)
  • Electron-wrapped IDE writing through a Chromium child process
  • Pen-test/IR replay of the PoC in a lab
Response runbook
Triage: pull the SHA256 of the written file and `git diff` HEAD vite.config.* on the dev host. Step 2 — contain: kill the node Vitest watcher (it auto-reloads), revert config from VCS, block inbound 63315. Step 3 — hunt: look for child processes of node.exe in the next 5 minutes (shell, certutil, curl, powershell), and pivot on the same SHA256 across the org.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","playwright.exe","headless_shell.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("playwright.exe","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.cjs","vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","playwright.exe","headless_shell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts for HTTP/WebSocket requests against the Vitest Browser API URL path that carries the CDP RPC channel, including the tester-role connection string described in the advisory's reproduction. vite/vitest config write quickly followed by node child-process spawn (T1546 trigger) AIInstallation High
Correlates a vite.config.* / vitest.config.* file modification with a node.exe invocation running vitest within the next 10 seconds on the same host — the post-overwrite RCE trigger described in the advisory ('Vitest reloaded the changed config and executed attacker-controlled Node.js code'). Rationale: Sequence (browser-written config → node re-spawn within seconds) is the exact RCE trigger called out in the advisory. Time-window join makes this far higher fidelity than either single event. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer editing config in an IDE that triggers an immediate Vitest hot-reload
  • Git checkout / branch switch that updates the config and reruns watch mode
  • Renovate/Dependabot autoformatter touching config followed by CI re-run
  • npm-install postinstall hooks that touch vitest config

| where not (FwInitiator in~ ("code.exe","webstorm64.exe","idea64.exe","git.exe","prettier.exe","eslint.exe","node.exe"))
Response runbook
Triage: inspect the diff of the written vite.config.* — look for unexpected require('child_process'), fs.write*, process.env exfil, or network calls. Step 2 — contain: kill node/Vitest watcher, isolate host from network, snapshot for forensics. Step 3 — hunt: pull node.exe's children from the host for the next 30 minutes and grep across the org for the same SHA256 on any vite.config.* file (drop the hash into ThreatIntelligenceIndicator).

Browser process loading @vitest / @playwright node_modules image AIExploitation Medium
Detects DLL/script image loads of @vitest or @playwright modules into Chromium-family browser processes — abnormal: the Vitest runtime should live in node.exe, not the browser. An image-load crossover is a strong sign the CDP bridge has been pivoted into a renderer-context exploit. Rationale: Browser binaries don't legitimately import Node-side @vitest or @playwright modules — these belong to the Node host. A cross-process image-load is article-specific because the advisory documents the CDP RPC bridging the two contexts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Electron VS Code extensions for Vitest UI loading shared module paths
  • Playwright headless_shell auto-instrumenting
  • Bundler dev-server proxying node_modules through Chromium for HMR
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "code.exe" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "code.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: confirm whether the host runs an Electron dev tool that legitimately hosts Vitest UI. Step 2 — contain: if not, isolate host, kill browser+node, snapshot. Step 3 — hunt: correlate with vitest config writes (UC3/UC5) and inbound 63315 (UC2) on the same host.

Vitest started with allowWrite/allowExec=false but no CDP restriction (false-sense-of-security config) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for node/Vitest invocations that look 'hardened' (--browser.api.allowWrite=false / allowExec=false) yet leave the CDP bridge enabled — the exact false-sense-of-security configuration the advisory says is exploitable. Pivots on the unique flag combination from the PoC. Rationale: Mirrors the advisory's reproduction config (allowWrite/allowExec=false) — the exact 'thought-it-was-safe' surface. Negation on a hypothetical CDP-disable flag keeps it future-proof if Vitest ships the patch. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer pasted PoC config from the advisory for triage
  • CI matrix sweeping multiple security flag combinations
  • Vitest's own e2e test suite covering the disabled paths
  • Auditing scripts probing for the vulnerable config
Response runbook
Triage: confirm Vitest version (>=3.0.0,<=3.2.4 / >=4.0.0,<=4.1.7 / 5.0.0-beta.0..3 are vulnerable). Step 2 — contain: kill the process, upgrade @vitest/browser, ensure Browser Mode binds to loopback. Step 3 — hunt: cross-reference with UC1/UC2 for the same host to confirm whether the API was also network-exposed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","pnpm.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","npx.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","@vitest/browser","vite-plus")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("allowWrite=false","allowExec=false")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("allowCDP=false","allowCdp=false","disableCDP"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\yarn.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\npx.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("vitest","@vitest/browser")
| where CommandLine has_any ("allowWrite=false","allowExec=false")
| where not(CommandLine has_any ("allowCDP=false","allowCdp=false"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound 63315 followed by file drop in Vitest project root (delivery → write chain) AIDelivery Medium
Correlates an inbound connection to the Vitest Browser Mode listener (port 63315) with a subsequent file create/modify in a project directory (vite-config-like paths, node_modules, test dirs) within a tight window — the delivery + drop chain implied by the advisory before config-overwrite RCE fires. Rationale: Combines the advisory's listener port (63315) with the file-staging step it implies, while remaining loose enough on the file path (project subtree) to catch payload variants that aren't just vite.config. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer git pull / npm install on a host with Vitest watch running
  • HMR-triggered file writes during legitimate test sessions
  • Internal LAN test runner pushing fixture files during a Vitest run
  • IDE auto-save during active Vitest watch mode
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hmr","--watch","hot"))
Response runbook
Triage: confirm SourceIP is unexpected (external / DMZ / unknown LAN peer). Step 2 — contain: drop inbound 63315 at host firewall, kill node + browser, snapshot dropped files. Step 3 — hunt: pivot on SourceIP to find any other dev hosts contacted on 63315, and grep the dropped files' SHA256 across the org via DeviceFileEvents.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email. The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] INFINITERED REDCap backdoor SHA256 hash sweep · [LLM] Trojanized REDCap PHP system-file modification (INFINITERED install) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to UNC6508 C2 infrastructure (23.169.65.49) · [LLM] Anomalous HTTP cookie payload to REDCap endpoints (INFINITERED C2 channel) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] UNC6508 Google Workspace content compliance rule BCC'ing to external Gmail · [LLM] Bulk Gmail export / Takeout immediately following Workspace admin rule change · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
UNC6508 Google Workspace content compliance rule BCC'ing to external Gmail AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core UNC6508 exfiltration TTP: a domain content compliance rule that silently BCCs keyword-matching mail to an external Gmail address. Pivots on the misspelled rule name 'Patroit' and the article's distinctive keyword 'chikungunya', plus generic markers (external Gmail target, admin-context create-email-setting events). Rationale: Anchored on three article-specific markers: misspelled rule name 'Patroit', the chikungunya keyword (UNC6508 collection priority specific to Guangdong 2025 outbreak), and the BCC-to-external-Gmail pattern GTIG flags as novel for a China-linked actor. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty — Workspace admin audit doesn't ship to those sources.
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1098.002 T1020
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DLP/compliance team standing up a legitimate keyword-monitoring rule that BCCs a quarantine mailbox
  • Legal/eDiscovery hold being implemented via content compliance
  • Migration to a new email security vendor that uses BCC routing for inspection
  • Shared-mailbox alias migration where mail is mirrored to a secondary Gmail account
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("dlp-admin","compliance@","ediscovery@") and RawData has_any ("hold","quarantine","legal"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full rule definition from Workspace admin audit: who created it, source IP/geo, what keywords, what BCC/forward destination, whether it survives MFA. Confirm the destination address is attacker-owned (not org-controlled). 2) Contain — delete the compliance rule, force-revoke the admin account session, rotate admin credentials and require phishing-resistant MFA. Block the BCC destination at the gateway. 3) Hunt — enumerate every content compliance / routing / forwarding rule across the domain (last 24 months) for external destinations; review admin audit for any rule edits by the same actor; pivot on the IP to other admin sessions; check REDCap servers for INFINITERED IOCs (see UC2/UC3).

INFINITERED REDCap backdoor SHA256 hash sweep AIInstallation Medium
IOC sweep for the seven INFINITERED SHA256 hashes published by GTIG. Hits process executions, file writes, image loads, and historical alert evidence — covers Linux/Windows REDCap hosts and any pivot host the trojanized payloads land on. Rationale: Verbatim use of GTIG-published SHA256 IOCs for INFINITERED. These are confirmed-bad — pure IOC match is appropriate. Sweeping file/process/image-load tables in parallel covers both the trojanized REDCap PHP loader and any downstream pivot binaries.

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher/analyst handling the IOC sample in a sandbox VM
  • DFIR responder copying a sample for analysis
  • Threat-intel tooling preloading hash IOCs into a vault directory
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\Sandbox\\","/sandbox/","/quarantine/","\\IR-Vault\\","/opt/ir-tools/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm the host is a REDCap server or has a network path to one. Pull the file path: an INFINITERED hash inside /var/www/.../redcap/ or %INETPUB%\redcap\ is a confirmed compromise, not a lab artefact. Check creation/modification time vs the host's last REDCap upgrade window. 2) Contain — isolate the server, snapshot disk + memory, take REDCap offline, force-rotate every credential that ever touched the login page (database, service, integration accounts) and every domain account that touched the server. 3) Hunt — enumerate REDCap PHP files modified since the earliest hash hit; pivot on the C2 IP 23.169.65.49 across DNS/network logs (UC3); review Google Workspace admin audit for content compliance rule changes (UC1); pull database tables that may store the harvested encrypted credentials.
